nameStory: The Virginian rose gets its name from the state of Virginia, where early botanists first formally described this native beauty. Despite its name suggesting a southern origin, this hardy rose actually ranges throughout eastern North America and is New England's most common wild rose!
description: The Virginian rose is a deciduous shrub that typically grows 3-6 feet tall, spreading by underground runners to form colonies. Its stems are armed with sharp, curved prickles, and it produces glossy compound leaves with 7-9 leaflets. In summer, fragrant pink flowers bloom singly or in small clusters, followed by bright red rose hips that persist into winter.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five-petaled pink flowers about 2 inches across with a sweet, classic rose fragrance. The petals feel papery-thin and may have a slight notch at the tip, surrounding a cluster of bright yellow stamens in the center.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 7-9 glossy, oval leaflets that feel smooth and slightly waxy to the touch. Each leaflet has finely toothed edges and the leaves turn spectacular shades of yellow, orange, and red in fall.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Bright red, round rose hips about the size of a small cherry that feel firm when ripe. They have a slightly sweet-tart taste and contain several hard seeds inside the fleshy exterior.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms spreading colonies through underground runners, creating dense thickets. The canes arch gracefully and can root where they touch the ground, helping the plant colonize new areas.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Armed with numerous sharp, curved prickles that hook backward like tiny thorns. The prickles feel needle-sharp and can easily snag clothing or skin when brushing against the plant.

habitat: Look for Virginian rose in sunny to partly shaded areas like field edges, roadsides, coastal dunes, and forest clearings throughout New England. It thrives in well-drained soils but tolerates various conditions from sandy to clay. You'll often find it forming thickets along shorelines, in old pastures, and at the edges of woodlands.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as compound leaflets unfurling from reddish buds. The glossy green foliage provides the first clue to identification before flowers appear.
seasonality.summer: Pink flowers bloom from June through August, appearing over an extended period rather than all at once. The sweet fragrance is strongest on warm, humid days.
seasonality.fall: This rose puts on one of nature's best autumn shows, with leaves turning brilliant yellows, oranges, and reds that persist for weeks. Bright red rose hips ripen and become a key identification feature.
seasonality.winter: Persistent red rose hips remain on bare stems, along with the characteristic curved prickles. The arching, reddish-brown canes and colonial growth pattern help identify it even when leafless.

funFact: Virginian rose hips contain more vitamin C than oranges - about 60 times more! During World War II, British schoolchildren were organized to collect rose hips to make vitamin C syrup when citrus fruits were scarce due to wartime rationing.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other wild roses, especially Carolina rose and swamp rose. Virginian rose typically has 7-9 leaflets (Carolina rose usually has 5-7) and grows in drier sites than swamp rose. Memory trick: "Virginia's got more leaflets to vote with" - referring to its higher leaflet count.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this native beauty with the invasive multiflora rose that's taking over many New England landscapes. While both are roses, the multiflora rose has clusters of small white flowers and forms much more aggressive, impenetrable thickets that crowd out native plants.
compareHints: Among New England's wild roses, Virginian rose stands out for its glossy leaflets (rugosa rose has wrinkled leaves) and typically 7-9 leaflets per leaf (most others have fewer). It also has some of the most spectacular fall color of any wild rose, turning multiple brilliant colors simultaneously rather than just yellow or brown.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England roses, multiflora rose is unique for its enormous flower clusters (other roses have flowers in smaller groups or singly) and those telltale fringed stipules.
Rugosa rose stands apart from other New England roses with its unmistakable wrinkled leaves - no other rose species has this corrugated texture.

Among New England's wild roses, swamp rose is unique in its preference for wet habitats - while Carolina rose and Virginia rose stick to drier areas, and multiflora rose (an invasive) has much denser thorns and forms larger, more aggressive colonies.
Among New England's wild roses, Carolina rose is the champion spreader, forming low colonies while relatives like swamp rose grow taller and more upright.

Among New England's roses, Sherard's downy-rose stands out for its compact size and distinctly grayish, downy leaves - most other wild roses like swamp rose or Carolina rose have greener, smoother foliage.

Among New England's wild roses, smooth rose is unique for its nearly thornless stems – multiflora rose has curved thorns, rugosa rose has dense straight prickles, and swamp rose has scattered thorns along its stems.
Among New England's roses, dog-rose stands out for its large, curved thorns and smooth leaflets without fuzzy coating.
Memorial rose is unique among New England roses for its prostrate, ground-hugging growth habit - all other rose species in the region grow as upright shrubs.
Among New England's wild roses, shining rose is uniquely low-growing and has by far the glossiest leaves.
Unlike the common multiflora rose with its clusters of small white flowers, cinnamon rose has larger, solitary pink blooms.
Among New England's wild roses, prickly wild rose stands out for its extreme thorniness — it has far more prickles per inch than rugosa rose, swamp rose, or any of our other native roses.
Among New England's roses, sweet-brier is the only one with apple-scented leaves - this fragrance alone separates it from multiflora rose, rugosa rose, and native species.
Climbing prairie rose stands out from other New England roses primarily by its vigorous climbing habit with long, flexible canes.
Unlike New England's native roses such as swamp rose or Carolina rose which have green leaves, red-leaved rose's blue-gray to purplish foliage is unmistakable.
